Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being reminded of the event by others
I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities
Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Negative Appraisals.value: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I have to be on guard all the time

vignette:
At 22, Lila had been married less than a year when she was sexually assaulted on her way home after a late shift at the call center where she worked. The assault happened near a service road behind a hospital complex, where the noise of an ambulance arriving cut across the dark parking area just as a man approached her. What stayed with her most was not a single orderly memory but flashes: the metallic taste in her mouth, the blare of the siren, a shoulder turning toward her too fast, hands and pavement and pieces that would not join into one complete sequence. When the memory came back later, it did not feel like remembering in any ordinary sense. It felt more real than the rest of her day, as if she were dropped back into the scene and could taste again what she had tasted then. Because the memory returned in that raw, sensory way, ordinary things began to take on the force of warning signs; the siren of an ambulance, a man turning abruptly, even the pressure in her chest during a busy shift seemed tied to the assault before she had consciously made the connection. Because those fragments returned with such force, she began to find pieces of the assault in more and more corners of daily life; after a bad spell of remembering, even ordinary sirens, abrupt movement, or the press of work tension could strike her as loaded before she had time to think. Afterward, she would sit with the conviction that if a memory could overtake her so completely, there had to be something wrong with her, something weak in her that would keep her from coping when it mattered.

In the weeks afterward, she found that certain moments in daily life could pull those fragments forward with frightening force. An ambulance passing her apartment or near the call center did not just remind her of the assault; it seemed to bring back the sensory intensity of it. Each time that happened, the reminder seemed to tell her something damning about herself: that she was the kind of person who could be overtaken at any moment, and that whatever had once made her feel competent or steady was gone. Each time one of those moments caught her, the thought came with it that this was what she had become now-someone flimsy, easily undone, no longer able to manage ordinary life the way other people could. Periods of pressure at work, when calls stacked up and supervisors monitored response times, made her body tense in the same way and the memory returned in disconnected pieces. Once she had come to see herself as the kind of person who could be overwhelmed without warning, ordinary moments no longer stayed ordinary for long; a supervisor's brisk tone, footsteps behind her in the corridor, or a stranger shifting suddenly in her peripheral vision could all snag her attention as signs that something was about to happen. Seeing happy families in the mall food court near her office or in advertisements left her abruptly shaken and ashamed, with the sense that everyone else belonged to a safe world she had somehow fallen out of. In those moments she had come to believe that if she let herself think directly about what happened, she would not be able to handle it. The memories felt so vivid and overpowering that they seemed to prove she was weak, inadequate, and no longer someone who could trust herself to stay composed.

Those beliefs began to organize her days. Because she was certain she had to stay on guard all the time, Lila entered every room already looking for exits, whether it was the break room at work, a restaurant with her husband, or a clinic waiting area. Unexpected movement beside her made her jerk hard in her chair or turn with her heart pounding before she knew what she was doing. She watched faces, doorways, uniforms, and corners automatically, convinced that danger could appear without warning if she relaxed even briefly. The more she saw herself as someone who could not cope and had to remain hyperalert, the more authority figures themselves began to feel loaded with danger; supervisors at the call center, security personnel in the lobby, and anyone in uniform could set her on edge before anything even happened.

She responded by shrinking her world in ways that made immediate sense to her. If a coworker started talking about crime, hospitals, or anything that might touch the assault, she would abruptly leave or change the subject to avoid being reminded by others. At work she kept her distance from floor managers and tried not to make eye contact with security guards near the entrance, timing her breaks to avoid passing them if she could. At home, when tension built to an unbearable level, she sometimes turned quickly toward sexual fantasies or sexual activity, not out of desire so much as from a desperate need to discharge the agitation in her body and replace the assault with something she could control. Each of these strategies was tied to the same conviction: that thinking or feeling too much about the event would overwhelm her.

But the things she did to get away from the memory seemed only to keep it raw. Because she cut off conversations, avoided reminders, and refused to look directly at what had happened, the assault remained in jagged fragments, returning without context and with full sensory force. After nights when she tried to manage her distress through sexual activity, she often felt hollow and more inadequate afterward, as if she had confirmed something damaged about herself. Avoiding supervisors and uniforms made those encounters rarer, but also more potent; a glimpse of a security officer at the call center doors could set off immediate scanning, and the ambulance bay behind the building became a route she would go far out of her way not to pass. Never staying in those moments long enough to learn that nothing was about to happen, she was left with the feeling that her precautions were the only thing holding danger back, which kept the sense of threat as high as ever. In this way, the very habits she relied on to get through the day kept teaching her that danger was still immediate and that only constant vigilance and escape were keeping her safe. Even happy families began to register less as ordinary scenes than as cues for what she believed she had lost, which made those images sting on sight.

Over months, the loop tightened. The more she scanned for danger, the more movement and emergency sounds caught her attention. The more she avoided, the more easily reminders broke through when she could not control them. Her husband noticed she always chose the seat facing the exit and startled when he came up beside her in the kitchen. At work her concentration slipped because she was tracking the room instead of the calls, and she had begun considering quitting after a panic-filled afternoon when an ambulance siren outside the building brought back the taste in her mouth so vividly she had to lock herself in the restroom. Seeking help now, Lila says what frightens her most is that if she ever stops guarding herself, it will happen again-or that if she allows the memory to come fully, she will fall apart completely. What she hopes, more quietly, is to feel present with her husband and move through an ordinary workday without bracing for danger at every turn.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not clearly state that triggers themselves lead to Lila’s negative appraisals, rather than co-occurring with shame or overwhelm.
Although memories are described as vivid and overpowering, no paragraph explicitly links the memory as causing her negative beliefs about being weak, inadequate, or unable to cope.
The vignette shows triggers bringing back memory, but does not explicitly convey that the trauma memory itself leads to or creates triggers/reminders.
It does not explicitly state that Lila’s maladaptive strategies increase or generate her sense of threat, even though avoidance and scanning are described as maintaining the cycle.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly state that triggers themselves lead to Lila’s negative appraisals, rather than co-occurring with shame or overwhelm.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: Although memories are described as vivid and overpowering, no paragraph explicitly links the memory as causing her negative beliefs about being weak, inadequate, or unable to cope.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette shows triggers bringing back memory, but does not explicitly convey that the trauma memory itself leads to or creates triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: It does not explicitly state that Lila’s maladaptive strategies increase or generate her sense of threat, even though avoidance and scanning are described as maintaining the cycle.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."

At work she kept her distance from floor managers and tried not to make eye contact with security guards near the entrance, timing her breaks to avoid passing them if she could. At home, when tension built to an unbearable level, she sometimes turned quickly toward sexual fantasies or sexual activity, not out of desire so much as from a desperate need to discharge the agitation in her body and replace the assault with something she could control. Each of these strategies was tied to the same conviction: that thinking or feeling too much about the event would overwhelm her.

But the things she did to get away from the memory seemed only to keep it raw. Because she cut off conversations, avoided reminders, and refused to look directly at what had happened, the assault remained in jagged fragments, returning without context and with full sensory force. After nights when she tried to manage her distress through sexual activity, she often felt hollow and more inadequate afterward, as if she had confirmed something damaged about herself. Avoiding supervisors and uniforms made those encounters rarer, but also more potent; a glimpse of a security officer at the call center doors could set off immediate scanning, and the ambulance bay behind the building became a route she would go far out of her way not to pass. Never staying in those moments long enough to learn that nothing was about to happen, she was left with the feeling that her precautions were the only thing holding danger back, which kept the sense of threat as high as ever. In this way, the very habits she relied on to get through the day kept teaching her that danger was still immediate and that only constant vigilance and escape were keeping her safe. Even happy families began to register less as ordinary scenes than as cues for what she believed she had lost, which made those images sting on sight.

Over months, the loop tightened. The more she scanned for danger, the more movement and emergency sounds caught her attention. The more she avoided, the more easily reminders broke through when she could not control them. Her husband noticed she always chose the seat facing the exit and startled when he came up beside her in the kitchen. At work her concentration slipped because she was tracking the room instead of the calls, and she had begun considering quitting after a panic-filled afternoon when an ambulance siren outside the building brought back the taste in her mouth so vividly she had to lock herself in the restroom. Seeking help now, Lila says what frightens her most is that if she ever stops guarding herself, it will happen again—or that if she allows the memory to come fully, she will fall apart completely. What she hopes, more quietly, is to feel present with her husband and move through an ordinary workday without bracing for danger at every turn.
